episodes.205340: An early September moisture surge resulted in the return of a more active weather pattern to Utah, including some isolated instances of flash flooding as well as a strong thunderstorm wind gust.
episodes.205347: A surface cold front stationed across west-central Pennsylvania produced scattered thunderstorms into central and eastern Pennsylvania during the afternoon and evening hours of September 4, 2025. Thunderstorms remained strong-to-severe across north-central Pennsylvania, producing isolated wind damage. Shear in the lowest levels allowed for a brief, weak tornado to form in Lancaster County.
episodes.205399: A potent cold front swept through Middle Tennessee during the evening of September 5, 2025. With an unstable and moist atmosphere ahead of this feature, the front provided additional lift to aid in the development of thunderstorms. These thunderstorms were able to become severe, producing large hail and damaging winds. The largest hail reported during this event was tennis ball size hail in Gainesboro with numerous reports of downed trees received throughout Middle Tennessee.
episodes.206006: Heavy monsoon rain caused stream rises and flash flooding in the Grand Canyon area.
episodes.206510: Increasingly unstable atmospheric conditions on the afternoon of September 5th ahead of a cold front led to strong thunderstorms across portions of West Virginia. Storms initially developed west of the Ohio River and grew to strong to severe thresholds as they crossed into the state. As a result, damaging wind gusts that accompanied these storms caused a swath of downed trees across the Kanawha Valley and up into the central lowlands before weakening as they approached the Appalachian Mountains.
episodes.207064: An upper-level trough moving through the area providing strong upper-level ascent combined with MLCAPE values between 1500-3000 J/kg and PWAT values between 1.8-2.0 (associated with the remnants of Tropical Cyclone Lorena) resulted in numerous showers and thunderstorms across much of western AZ and southern CA. A cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon hours over Yuma County and slowly moved westward, reaching the Lower Colorado River Valley before dissipating. With this cluster of storms, damaging winds, flash flooding and areas of dense blowing dust were observed with the City of Yuma area seeing the most impacts.
episodes.207118: A smattering of weak showers and storms moved across the northern Panhandles on September 4th, in an environment favorable for downburst winds. A few stronger wind gusts, even up to 60mph, occurred with these showers thanks to some drier air in the lower levels of the atmosphere.
episodes.207246: An upper-level trough moving through the area providing strong upper-level ascent combined with MLCAPE values between 1500-3000 J/kg and PWAT values between 1.8-2.0 (associated with the remnants of Tropical Cyclone Lorena) resulted in numerous showers and thunderstorms across much of western AZ and southern CA. A cluster of strong to severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon hours over Yuma County and slowly moved westward, reaching the Lower Colorado River Valley before dissipating. With this cluster of storms, damaging winds, flash flooding and areas of dense blowing dust were observed with the Yuma area seeing the most impacts.
episodes.207273: As a cold front pushed east through central Kentucky, a line of scattered thunderstorms developed. One storm just north of the Tennessee border brought a few trees down as it moved east as another storm passing near Richmond blew trees down in an isolated area.
episodes.207374: Tropical Storm Lorena's remnants, a late-summer cold front, and an upper-level trough collectively contributed to significant thunderstorm activity across North Texas during the afternoon and evening of September 5th and into the morning of September 6th. Several of these storms generated damaging wind gusts and hail, while frequent cloud-to-ground lightning resulted in multiple residential fires.
episodes.207381: Evening thunderstorms within northeast flow enhanced by the sea breeze over the area between weak Eastern Seaboard surface ridging extending into the northern gulf and a lingering Western Atlantic surface trough produce a waterspout and strong marine wind gust near the mouth of Tampa Bay.
episodes.207526: Steady moisture return and strong heating ahead of an approaching cold front set the stage for thunderstorm development near the Tennessee River during the late afternoon on September 5, 2025.  An isolated severe storm produced damaging winds in Henderson County.
episodes.207572: Tropical moisture associated with a tropical wave and other trade wind perturbations, along with an upper-level trough resulted in the formation of strong showers and thunderstorms. These showers resulted in flooding, landslide and wind damage along portions of eastern, northern and western Puerto Rico.
episodes.207641: In the early morning hours of the 5th, a deep low pressure passing near the Bay of Green Bay caused wind gusts to briefly gust to 58 mph at Minneapolis Shoal.
episodes.207726: A stationary boundary north of the area and passing mid-level shortwave trough combined with the afternoon sea breeze to produce strong thunderstorms on September 5, 2025.
episodes.207828: On September 4th, precipitable water values increased to above normal values, with the 18z Grand Junction sounding showing 0.69 inches of precipitable water. To the west of eastern Utah and western Colorado, an area of weak rotation associated with a passing shortwave helped to provide extra lift. Morning sunshine helped to realized enough instability that, with all other factors present, thunderstorms developed over the higher terrain through the afternoon. These storms were capable of producing heavy rain, were not especially fast moving, and had a tendency to train over the same area for several hours.
episodes.207838: Multiple clusters of thunderstorms developed and moved southeast ahead of a cold front across east Tennessee and western North Carolina throughout the evening. Several storms produced brief severe weather throughout western NC.
episodes.207866: A push of monsoon moisture fueled scattered thunderstorms, with the greatest activity on the 5th and 6th. Many storms produced severe weather and flash flooding.
episodes.207867: A push of monsoon moisture fueled isolated thunderstorms for several days. A few produced severe weather and flash flooding.
episodes.207868: A push of monsoon moisture fueled scattered thunderstorms, many of which produced severe weather and flash flooding.

Thunderstorms developed over the Redlands area of Grand Junction late in the afternoon of September 4th, and remained there for 2-3 hours. Impacts began to be noticed around 6:45 PM MDT, with an LSR in the area of 1 ESE Redlands indicating Water out of the banks of nearby wash and running over Redlands Parkway in several areas. Approximately half an hour later, another LSR indicated that water running over the roadway in many areas along South Camp Road in the Redlands (Redlands 1SSE). Debris was also reported as having to be removed from Monument Road (Redlands 3SSE). In addition to the LSR'd events, properties were flooded, normally dry washes were overfilled, and water and debris inundated several roadways in the area. Additionally, social media reports indicated flooding along No Thoroughfare Canyon, Monument Road, and in the Devil's Kitchen area of Colorado National Monument. Once the rain stopped and the storms dissipated, a local spotter provided the total precipitation from this storm, which was a 2.33 inches.
